result:
I like the idea that a city has two maps. One shows streets, stations, bridges, and the names of parks. The other is invisible: where someone received good news, where a friendship began, where a person sat quietly until the worst hour of their life became an hour they survived.

On this second map, a corner bakery might be more important than city hall. A bench might carry the weight of a cathedral. The bus stop outside a pharmacy might mark the exact place someone decided to forgive their father, although the father never knew and the bus arrived late.

We move through these hidden landscapes every day, usually without noticing. The woman buying oranges may be rehearsing an apology. The man walking a stubborn dog may have just learned he will become a grandfather. Someone staring at a puddle may simply like how the clouds look broken and repairable.

This is why I distrust the phrase “nothing happened today.” Something almost always happened. A plant tilted toward the window. A child discovered that shadows cannot be picked up. Somebody made a meal from what remained in the cupboard and found it unexpectedly good. The world performed its quiet maintenance.

Perhaps attention is a modest form of gratitude. Not constant amazement, not an obligation to turn every moment into a lesson. Just looking long enough to let ordinary things become particular. This cup. That laugh. The warm rectangle of sunlight on the floor, waiting for no one and welcoming anyone.
